Live Dealer Casino Games: How They Actually Work

Published August 28, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

A live dealer table looks almost identical to a regular online casino game from the player's chair: cards get dealt, a wheel spins, chips move. What's different is everything behind the screen. A real person is shuffling and dealing from a physical studio somewhere, a camera rig is streaming that action in real time, and a layer of software is quietly translating what happens on the table into the numbers your account balance runs on. Understanding that pipeline is the difference between treating live dealer games as "the same thing with video added" and actually knowing what changes.

Inside a live dealer studio

Live dealer games are filmed on purpose-built sets, usually run by specialist gaming-technology studios rather than by the casino brand itself, then licensed out to multiple operators. A single studio floor typically holds several tables running at once — blackjack, roulette, baccarat — each staffed by a trained dealer and covered by multiple camera angles: a wide shot of the whole table, a tight overhead shot for card and chip detail, and sometimes a dedicated angle on the wheel or shoe. Lighting, felt color, and camera placement are all standardized because the video feed has to remain legible on everything from a large desktop monitor to a phone screen.

Dealers work in shifts like any other casino staff, following scripted pacing and house procedures for shuffling, dealing, and handling disputes, with pit supervisors present off-camera the same way they would be on a physical casino floor.

How the table gets turned into data

The interesting engineering problem isn't the video — it's converting physical events into a data feed the platform can settle bets against instantly and accurately. Roulette wheels used in live dealer setups are typically fitted with a sensor that reads exactly where the ball lands, removing any ambiguity about the result. Card values are usually read by optical recognition software trained on the studio's specific deck design, cross-checked in real time so a misread card gets caught before it ever reaches a player's screen. Chips and bets, by contrast, are almost always tracked entirely on the software side — you're clicking or tapping to place a wager on your own device, and that bet is matched against the physical outcome the cameras and sensors just captured.

That combination — real, physical randomness plus a verification layer that turns it into clean data instantly — is what live dealer games are actually selling: not just video of a casino, but a system built to make sure the video and the settled result always match.

Why the math isn't identical to an RNG version

It's a common assumption that a live dealer blackjack table and an RNG blackjack game with the same rules pay out identically over time. The rules-driven house edge can indeed be very close if the number of decks, payout on blackjack, and dealer-stands-on-soft-17 rule all match — but a few things routinely differ in practice. Live tables sometimes carry slightly different rule sets than a platform's RNG version of the same game, and live dealer tables frequently offer additional side bets (perfect pairs, lucky ladies, various baccarat or roulette side wagers) that carry a meaningfully higher house edge than the base game and exist specifically to boost revenue on a slower-paced format. None of that changes the math of the base game itself, but it does mean the two aren't automatically interchangeable just because they share a name.

Pace matters too, in a way that's easy to overlook. A live table dealing perhaps 30-40 hands an hour, versus an RNG table capable of well over 200, means your total wagered amount over a given session is naturally lower at the same bet size — which affects your session-level variance and expected loss, even though the underlying per-hand edge hasn't moved. For a deeper look at how house edge is calculated in the first place, see our house edge guide.

Worth remembering: the game you're watching is real, but the rules printed on the table — deck count, payouts, side-bet odds — are still what determines the math, exactly like an RNG version. Slower play doesn't change the edge; it changes how much of it you're exposed to per hour.

The common live dealer formats

Live dealer blackjack, roulette, and baccarat are the three formats that show up across most licensed platforms, generally following the same rules as their RNG counterparts with a human dealer running the table. Beyond those staples, a growing category of game-show-style live formats has emerged — large spinning wheels with multiplier segments, bonus rounds hosted by a live presenter, and other formats built specifically for the live video format rather than adapted from a traditional table game. These game-show titles typically carry their own distinct odds structure, often with a wider spread between the most common (low) and rarest (high-multiplier) outcomes than a traditional table game would ever produce.

What to know before you sit down at one

A few practical differences are worth knowing going in. Betting windows are timed — you'll usually see a countdown during which bets must be placed before the dealer deals or the wheel spins, and a missed window means waiting for the next round. Stream quality depends on your own connection as much as the studio's, and a brief buffering delay is normal rather than a sign anything's wrong with the game. Table minimums and maximums are frequently set differently from a platform's RNG tables of the same game, sometimes higher, reflecting the studio and staffing cost of running a live seat versus a purely software-driven one. And because a real dealer is running actual timing, live tables can't be sped up the way an RNG game can — if pace of play matters to your bankroll management, that's worth factoring in before choosing one format over the other.

Frequently asked questions

Is a live dealer game harder to rig than an RNG game?

Neither format is "easier" to rig on a licensed, regulated platform — both are subject to independent testing and auditing. Live dealer games add a physical verification layer (sensors, optical card recognition, camera coverage) specifically so the recorded outcome can be checked against what happened on camera.

Why do live dealer tables sometimes have higher minimum bets?

Running a live table involves studio space, camera equipment, and a paid dealer for every seat, which is a materially higher fixed cost per table than an RNG game. Operators often set higher minimums on live tables to offset that cost.

Can I chat with the dealer or other players?

Most live dealer platforms include a text chat feature where you can message the dealer directly, and on some tables, other players seated at the same game. Dealers are trained to keep the pace of play moving regardless of chat volume.

Do live dealer games have worse odds than RNG games?

Not inherently — the base game's house edge is set by the same rules (deck count, payouts) either way. Where live tables often differ is in higher-edge optional side bets and, at some platforms, slightly different base rules than the RNG version, so it's worth checking the specific table's rules rather than assuming they match.
